title: Tree pruning & crown reduction
hero: Tree pruning & crown reduction in Leicestershire.
excerpt: Cut properly, so the tree recovers. Reduction, thinning, crown lifting, deadwooding and pollarding across Leicestershire and the East Midlands — carried out to recognised arboricultural practice by climbers who've been doing it for decades.
seo_title: Tree Pruning & Crown Reduction in Leicestershire
seo_desc: Crown reduction, thinning, lifting and deadwooding by qualified arborists near Lutterworth and Hinckley. No topping, everything cleared. Free quotes.

faq.q: How much can you take off a tree?
faq.a: As a rule of thumb, no more than about a third of the crown in one go, and less on an older tree. Beyond that you're stressing it into heavy regrowth. If a tree genuinely needs more than that removing to solve the problem, removal and replanting is often the honest answer.

Correct pruning won't. Excessive or badly placed cuts can, especially on a tree already under stress from drought, compaction or root damage. That's the whole argument for using someone who does this for a living.

faq.q: My neighbour's tree overhangs my garden. What can I do?
faq.a: In England you're generally entitled to cut back growth to the boundary line, and the cuttings technically belong to your neighbour. But you can't trespass to do it, you can't destabilise or kill the tree, and TPO and conservation area rules still apply. In practice a conversation and a shared quote goes better than a chainsaw. We're happy to speak to both parties.

faq.q: Do you take the branches away?
faq.a: Yes — chipped on site, hardwood taken back to the yard for firewood, ground raked. It's included in the price.

content:
What pruning actually does

A tree that's grown too big for its space doesn't usually need removing. It needs the right cuts in the right places — enough to solve the problem, not so much that the tree spends the next three years throwing out panicked regrowth.

Good pruning takes weight off the ends of limbs rather than lopping through the middle of them. It keeps the tree's natural outline, leaves wounds small enough to seal over, and buys you five to ten years before anyone needs to look at it again. Bad pruning — topping, over-thinning, flush cuts — does the opposite, and you can see the results in gardens all over the county.

The five jobs people ask for

Crown reduction

Bringing the overall height and spread back by a measured amount, typically one to three metres, while keeping the shape. This is the answer to "it's blocking all our light" and "it's getting too close to the house". Reduction is specified as a distance, not a percentage guess, so you know exactly what you're getting.

Crown thinning

Selectively removing a proportion of the inner branches to let more light and wind through without changing the tree's size or outline. Useful for dense, heavy canopies — and for reducing sail area on exposed sites before winter.

Crown lifting

Taking the lowest branches off to raise the canopy — over a driveway, a path, a lawn you'd like to mow, or a road where a high-sided vehicle keeps catching. Usually the cheapest job on this list and often all that's needed.

Deadwooding

Removing dead, dying, diseased and broken branches from a mature tree. This is a safety job rather than a cosmetic one, and it's what we'd recommend for a big veteran oak or beech you want to keep exactly as it is.

Pollarding

A hard cut back to a previous pollard point, repeated on a cycle. It suits trees that have been managed that way historically — willows, limes, some poplars. It is not a technique for starting on a mature tree that has never been pollarded, whatever anyone tells you.

Topping is not pruning. Sawing a crown back to bare stubs leaves large wounds that never seal, invites decay into the trunk, and produces weakly attached regrowth that is more likely to fail in a storm than the original branches. We won't do it, and any quote that's suspiciously cheap is usually a quote for exactly this.

Before we cut anything

  • We check for a TPO. Tree Preservation Orders are common in Leicestershire, and work on a protected tree without consent is a criminal offence with fines to match. We check the council register as part of the visit.
  • We check conservation areas. If you're in one, six weeks' written notice to the council is required before most tree work — we'll tell you and help with the paperwork.
  • We check for nesting birds. All wild birds' nests are protected while in use. Roughly March to August we work around them, which occasionally means rescheduling.
  • We check for bats. Old trees with cavities can be roosts, and roosts are protected year-round.

Timing

Most broadleaf trees are best pruned in late autumn and winter, dormant and bare, when you can see the structure and the tree loses least. There are exceptions worth knowing:

  • Cherry, plum and other Prunus — prune in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf
  • Birch, maple and walnut — bleed heavily in late winter, so late summer is kinder
  • Fruit trees — winter for shape and vigour, summer to restrain growth
  • Anything dangerous — whenever it's dangerous. Safety beats season.

What it costs

Pruning is priced on access and complexity rather than height alone. A crown lift on an open front lawn is a couple of hours; a reduction on a mature beech overhanging a conservatory, with everything roped down and barrowed through the house-side gate, is a different job entirely.

We come out, look at it, and give you a written fixed price that includes chipping and clearing everything away. The visit costs nothing and there's no obligation.

title: Tree felling & removal
excerpt: Taken down in one where there's room, dismantled piece by piece where there isn't. Dead, dangerous, overgrown or in the wrong place — removed cleanly, with everything cleared away and the ground raked before we leave.
seo_title: Tree Felling & Removal in Leicestershire | Harbour Tree Care
seo_desc: Safe tree felling and removal near Lutterworth and Hinckley. Straight fells, section dismantling, dead and dangerous trees. Free quote, all cleared.

faq.q: Do I need permission to remove my own tree?
faq.a: Only if it's protected. If the tree has a Tree Preservation Order, or you're in a conservation area, you need the council's consent first — and doing it without can mean an unlimited fine. If it isn't protected, it's your tree and your decision. We check which applies as part of the free visit.

faq.q: Will you take the whole tree away?
faq.a: Yes, and it's in the price. Brash is chipped on site, cordwood comes back to our yard for firewood, and we rake the ground before we leave. You shouldn't have to look at a pile of logs for a fortnight.

faq.q: Can you remove a tree close to my house?
faq.a: That's most of what we do. A climber dismantles it in small sections, lowering each one on ropes, so nothing drops onto the roof, the conservatory or the fence. It takes longer than felling in the open, but it's controlled every step of the way.

Felling leaves a stump at ground level. If you want it gone — to lay turf, plant, pave or build — we grind it out separately. It's quicker and cheaper to do it in the same visit, so it's worth mentioning when you enquire. See stump grinding .

content:
Two ways a tree comes down

If there's clear space to drop it — an open field, a big garden with nothing underneath — the quickest and cheapest route is a straight fell: a hinge cut, a controlled drop, and the tree is on the ground in one piece to be cut up.

Most gardens don't have that space. Between the house, the shed, the fence and next door's greenhouse, there's nowhere safe for a whole tree to land. So a climber takes it down in sections, roping and lowering each limb and each length of trunk under control, until there's nothing left but a stump. It's slower, it's more skilled, and it's how the vast majority of our removals are done.

Which method suits your tree comes down to access and what's underneath it — and that's exactly what the free site visit is for.

Trees we're most often called to remove

  • Dead and dying trees — once a tree is dead the wood turns brittle and unpredictable, so these are best dealt with sooner rather than left another winter
  • Dangerous and storm-damaged trees — split limbs, cracked forks, a tree leaning after a gale. If it's an immediate hazard, see our emergency call-out
  • Ash dieback — now widespread across Leicestershire. Infected ash becomes brittle and dangerous to climb as the disease advances, so it's much safer and cheaper to deal with earlier
  • Trees that have outgrown the garden — the conifer planted as a hedge in the eighties, the leylandii now blocking all the light, the willow lifting the patio
  • Boundary and overhanging trees — where the sensible answer, and the neighbour conversation, both need handling with a bit of care

Does it actually need to come down? Sometimes a reduction or a crown lift solves the problem for a fraction of the cost and keeps the tree. We'll always tell you if that's the case — even when you rang us asking for a fell. It's the same principle that stops us topping trees.

Before we remove anything

  • We check for a Tree Preservation Order. Removing a protected tree without consent is a criminal offence with unlimited fines. We check the council register as part of the visit
  • We check conservation areas. Most work in one needs six weeks' written notice to the council first
  • We check for nesting birds and bat roosts, both protected by law. Roughly March to August we work around nesting season

If the tree is protected and the reason for removal is sound — it's dead, dangerous or diseased — that's usually a straightforward application, and we can handle it for you.

What happens to the timber

It doesn't go to landfill and it doesn't get left in a heap on your drive. Brash goes through the chipper on site, good hardwood comes back to the yard to be seasoned for firewood, and the ground is raked before we go. Clearing up is part of the quoted price, not an extra.

What removal costs

Price depends far more on access and risk than on the size of the tree. A tall tree in an open field can be cheaper than a modest one wedged behind a conservatory, because one is a straightforward fell and the other is a day of roping every piece out through a side gate. We quote a fixed price after seeing it — the prices page gives rough ranges so you're not going in blind.

title: Stump grinding
excerpt: The stump ground out below ground level, the roots chased back, and a bed of chippings left where the problem used to be. So you can turf it, plant it, pave it or build on it — and forget it was ever there.
seo_title: Stump Grinding in Leicestershire | Harbour Tree Care
seo_desc: Stump grinding near Lutterworth and Hinckley. Stumps ground out below ground level so you can turf, plant, pave or build. Free quote.

faq.a: Normally 15 to 30cm below ground level, which is plenty for turf, paving or general tidying. If you're planting a new tree or building, we go deeper and clear more root material — just tell us the plan when you enquire.

Grinding the stump and the top of the main roots stops regrowth for the vast majority of species. A few very vigorous trees can sucker from roots left in the ground, but removing the stump takes away the bulk of the energy store, so it's the reliable way to stop it coming back.

faq.q: What do you do with the woodchip?
faq.a: Your choice. We can rake it back into the hole and level it off — it makes decent mulch — or barrow it away and leave the ground clear for topsoil. Removing it is a small extra; raking it in is included.

faq.q: Can you grind a stump another company left?
faq.a: Yes, we do that regularly. It doesn't matter who took the tree down — if you've got a stump, we can grind it.

content:
Why a stump is more trouble than it looks

A stump seems harmless enough sitting there. In practice it's a slow nuisance: it trips people up on a dark evening, it throws up suckers and shoots that keep coming back, it gets in the way of a mower, and it quietly blocks any plan to lay a lawn, a patio or an extension over it.

Left in the ground it also rots, and a rotting stump can become a home for honey fungus — a root-rot that spreads underground and can go on to attack healthy plants and trees nearby. Grinding it out removes the food source along with the trip hazard.

How grinding works

A stump grinder is a machine with a rotating cutting wheel that chews the stump and the top of the main roots down into chippings, working from the top down to below ground level — typically 15 to 30cm down, deeper if you're planting or building. What's left is a hole full of woodchip and soil, which you can rake flat, barrow away, or backfill with topsoil ready for turf.

  • Ground out below the surface, not just cut flush
  • Roots chased back where access allows
  • The chippings raked level or removed — your choice
  • We grind stumps left behind by other firms, not just our own
  • Most machines fit through a standard side gate; we'll check access when we quote

Grinding, not digging. Digging a stump out by hand or with a machine bucket tears up the whole area and often can't get near roots under a wall or path. Grinding is cleaner, quicker, and works in tight spots a digger can't reach.

Planning to replant on the same spot?

Tell us when you enquire. If you want to plant a new tree where the old one stood, we grind deeper and clear more of the root material, because fresh roots don't establish well in a bed of old woodchip. A little extra grinding now saves a struggling replacement later.

What stump grinding costs

Usually priced per stump, by diameter, with the total depending on how many you've got and how easy they are to reach. Doing it in the same visit as a tree removal is cheaper than a separate call-out, so it's worth mentioning up front. The prices page gives rough ranges.

title: Site & plot clearance
excerpt: Overgrown gardens, self-set scrub, old hedge lines and whole development plots taken back to workable ground and cleared away — with the nesting-bird, protected-species and TPO checks done properly, so the job doesn't get stopped halfway.
seo_title: Site & Plot Clearance in Leicestershire | Harbour Tree Care
seo_desc: Site and plot clearance for developers, farms and estates near Lutterworth. Overgrown plots cleared, nesting and TPO checks handled. Free quote.
content:
Who we clear sites for

Site clearance covers a lot of ground, literally. For us it's usually one of these:

  • Developers and self-builders — an infill plot or a larger site that needs trees, scrub and hedge lines cleared before the groundworkers move in
  • Farms and estates — overgrown corners, gappy hedge lines, self-set ash and sycamore reclaiming a field edge
  • Homeowners — a garden that got away over a few wet summers, or a new house with an old jungle behind it
  • Commercial and public sites — schools, car parks, business premises where vegetation has taken over

Whatever the setting, the outcome is the same: cleared, level, workable ground with everything taken away.

What clearance involves

Depending on the site, that can mean felling and removing trees, cutting out leylandii and overgrown hedges, clearing scrub and bramble, grinding out stumps, and chipping or removing all the arisings. On a development plot we can grind stumps out so the ground is genuinely ready to build on, rather than leaving a field of obstacles for the digger.

The bit that catches people out: wildlife and protected trees. Clearing a site in nesting season without checking, or taking out a hedge or tree that turns out to be protected, can bring the council or an ecologist down on a project and stop it dead — sometimes with a prosecution attached. We check for TPOs, conservation area status, active nests and protected species before the machinery arrives, which is exactly what keeps a build on schedule.

Timing matters on clearance

Nesting bird season runs roughly March to August, and all active nests are protected by law — which can mean a large clearance has to wait or be surveyed first. If you've got a site to clear and a deadline to hit, the single best thing you can do is talk to us early, so the timing works around the wildlife rather than colliding with it.

For contractors and repeat clients

If you're a developer, builder or land agent who needs clearance done reliably and invoiced properly, we're set up for that — method statements and the paperwork you need for site, and a crew that turns up when it says it will. See our contact page to talk about a specific site, and tell us the deadline.

title: Tree surveys & reports
excerpt: A written assessment of a tree's condition, safety and likely future, produced by a qualified arborist — the document a planning officer, a lender, an insurer or a managing agent will accept.
seo_title: Tree Surveys & Reports in Leicestershire | Harbour Tree Care
seo_desc: Tree surveys, safety inspections and reports for planning, mortgages and insurers near Lutterworth and Hinckley. Qualified arborists. Free enquiry.
content:
When you need a tree report

Most people don't go looking for a tree survey — someone asks them for one. It's usually one of four situations:

  • Planning applications. Where trees on or near a development have to be assessed and protected before consent is granted. This is the report a local authority planning department expects, and getting it wrong holds up the whole application
  • Buying or selling a property. Where a surveyor, lender or insurer has flagged a tree near the building — often over subsidence worries on clay soils — and wants a professional opinion before the money moves
  • Duty of care. Schools, landlords, businesses, parish councils and managing agents have a legal responsibility for trees the public walks under. A periodic inspection is how you show you took reasonable care if a branch ever comes down
  • Insurance claims and disputes. Subsidence claims, storm-damage assessments, and boundary or neighbour disagreements where an independent expert view settles it

What a report gives you

A clear written assessment of each tree's species, condition, and any defects or safety concerns, with plain recommendations and timescales — what needs doing, how urgently, and what can safely be left. Where it's for planning, the report is prepared to the standard the planning system expects and includes the tree constraints and protection information the officer needs.

How it works

Tell us what the report is for and who's asked for it — that tells us which type of survey you actually need, which isn't always the one you were told to get. We visit, assess the trees, and produce the written report. If the survey turns up work that needs doing, we can quote for that separately; there's no obligation to have us do it.

title: Hedge cutting
excerpt: Trimmed, reduced and reshaped — from a garden boundary that's got out of hand to a long farm hedge line. Cut cleanly, cleared away, and left tidy.
seo_title: Hedge Cutting & Trimming in Leicestershire | Harbour Tree Care
seo_desc: Hedge cutting, trimming, height reduction and reshaping near Lutterworth and Hinckley — garden hedges, leylandii and farm hedge lines. Cuttings cleared. Free quote.
content:
The hedges we cut

  • Garden hedges — privet, beech, hornbeam, laurel and the rest, kept trimmed, square and healthy
  • Conifer hedges and leylandii — trimmed to keep them in check, or reduced in height where they've got away. (A word of caution below on how far a conifer can be cut back)
  • Overgrown and neglected hedges — brought back to a manageable size and shape over one or two cuts
  • Farm and estate hedge lines — longer boundary hedges maintained on a seasonal cycle

Trimming, reducing and reshaping

A routine trim keeps a hedge dense, tidy and the size you want it. A height or width reduction brings an overgrown hedge back under control — useful where it's taking light, blocking a path or outgrowing its spot. Reshaping a neglected hedge sometimes takes two sessions a season apart, so it thickens back up rather than being left bare.

One honest warning about conifers. Most conifers — leylandii especially — won't regrow from old brown wood. Cut the sides back past the green growth and you're left with bare brown patches that never green up again. We'll always tell you how far a conifer hedge can safely be taken in, and if it's really too big to reduce without ruining it, we'll say that too — sometimes removal and replanting is the honest answer.

Nesting season

Hedges are prime nesting habitat, and all active birds' nests are protected by law. Between roughly March and August we check before we cut, and where there's an active nest we'll work around it or come back — it's the law, and it's the right thing. Autumn and winter are the ideal time for a hard reduction anyway.

Cleared away, not left in a heap

The cuttings are chipped or taken away as part of the job. You get a tidy hedge and a clear path, not a mound of clippings to deal with yourself.

title: Seasoned firewood
excerpt: Hardwood logs from our own tree work, split and seasoned at the yard until they're dry enough to burn cleanly and hot. Delivered by the load around Lutterworth, Hinckley and the surrounding villages.
seo_title: Seasoned Firewood & Logs in Leicestershire | Harbour Tree Care
seo_desc: Seasoned hardwood logs from our own tree work, split, dried and delivered around Lutterworth, Hinckley and the villages. Order early for winter. Local delivery.

faq.q: How do I know the wood is dry enough?
faq.a: Properly seasoned wood is lighter than green wood, the ends are cracked and checked, and the bark comes away easily. The reliable test is a moisture meter — you want 20% or below. Wood at that level lights easily and burns without hissing or heavy smoke.
Late summer or early autumn is ideal — you get the pick of the well-seasoned wood before the winter rush. Leave it until the cold sets in and supply gets tight.

content:
Local wood, not imported

Every tree we take down produces timber, and the good hardwood doesn't go to waste — it comes back to the yard, gets cut and split, and is seasoned until it's ready to burn. When you buy a load, you're buying local timber that would otherwise be a by-product, not kiln-dried logs shipped halfway across Europe.

It's mostly mixed native hardwood — oak, ash, beech, sycamore and the like — which burns hotter and longer than softwood and is what you want in a wood burner or an open fire.

Properly seasoned means it actually burns

Freshly cut "green" wood can be half water by weight. Try to burn it and most of the heat goes into boiling that water off — you get a smoky, hissing, disappointing fire, a glassed-up stove door and a tarred-up chimney. Seasoned wood has been dried until the moisture is low enough to light easily and burn cleanly, giving you heat instead of steam.

Order early — genuinely

This isn't a sales line. Properly seasoned wood takes months to dry, and by the first cold snap in autumn everyone wants logs at once. Order in late summer and you'll have well-seasoned wood put by; leave it until November and the best of it is already spoken for.

content:
Tree work in and around Twycross

Twycross sits right on the Leicestershire–Warwickshire border, about a half-hour run from the yard at Ashby Magna, and it's country we've worked for years — the villages around the zoo, the farms and estates off the A444, and the lanes running down towards Sheepy and Sibson. Roy Harbour started the business in 1977, and plenty of the work out this way still comes from a word over a field gate.

What we get called out for locally

  • Mature parkland and estate trees — the big oaks, limes and beech on farms, paddocks and country gardens that want skilled reduction or deadwooding rather than a quick cut
  • Hedgerow and field-boundary trees — overgrown boundaries, roadside limbs on the lanes, and trees overhanging stock fencing and outbuildings
  • Ash dieback — widespread in the field boundaries and lanes around Twycross, and best dealt with while the timber is still safe to climb
  • Leylandii and conifer boundaries reduced, or taken out and the stumps ground
  • Storm damage after a gale — split limbs, trees down across tracks and lanes, branches on barns and sheds
  • Plot and site clearance for rural builders and barn conversions

Conservation areas and TPOs in Twycross

Twycross falls under Hinckley and Bosworth Borough Council, which holds the Tree Preservation Order register and conservation area boundaries for the parish. The outlying villages sit under North West Leicestershire or, over the border, North Warwickshire instead. If your tree is protected, consent is needed before work begins, and in a conservation area you must give six weeks' notice — we check which authority applies, and which rules, as part of the free site visit, and can put the application in on your behalf.
